title: India Just Abolished All Taxes on Foreign Bond Investment. One Billion Dollars Flowed In Within Three Days.
excerpt: The tax exemption and expanded market access are designed to lure back foreign capital and lock in a spot in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index. Here is what it means for NRI investors.
body:
India has scrapped withholding and capital gains taxes on foreign investments in government bonds, in a sweeping move that has already drawn more than $1 billion in new inflows within three trading sessions and significantly strengthened the country's case for inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index.

The measures, unveiled last Friday by the finance ministry and the Reserve Bank of India, go beyond tax relief. Policymakers also broadened the pool of government securities available to foreigners without investment limits through the Fully Accessible Route and introduced new incentives to encourage banks to raise foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians and for companies to tap overseas borrowings.

"We believe that these changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt and systematic fixed income at State Street Investment Management, which manages approximately $5.6 trillion in assets.

## What Changed and Why

The reforms were triggered by the oil shock that has battered Indian assets throughout 2026. With Brent crude hovering above $93 a barrel and the Iran-US conflict now in its fourth month, India's current account deficit has widened, foreign portfolio investors have pulled a record $30.4 billion from Indian equities this year, and the rupee has fallen 5.86 per cent — trailing only the Indonesian rupiah as Asia's worst-performing currency.

Before the announcement, just $1.6 billion in government debt had been purchased by foreign investors in the entire year-to-date period. The tax exemption, effective from 1 April 2026, applies to all interest income and capital gains earned by foreign portfolio investors on government securities. A similar exemption has been granted to the Bank for International Settlements.

Yields on government bonds have already fallen 10 to 30 basis points across the curve, with shorter maturities seeing the biggest declines. The relief has been most visible in the 5-year segment, where international buyers have been most active.

## The Bloomberg Index Play

For investors tracking global fixed income, the most consequential implication may be India's bid for inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index — one of the world's most widely tracked bond benchmarks.

Bloomberg Index Services is expected to seek investor feedback later this month on whether Indian government bonds should be added to its flagship index. India joined JPMorgan's emerging market debt index in June 2024, which brought predictable and durable inflows; inclusion in Bloomberg's broader gauge would significantly amplify that effect.

Niel Clement, portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management — which manages more than €1.6 trillion — said the tax reforms would redirect flows to the onshore market and provide a constructive boost to India's Bloomberg bid. M&G Investments added that index inclusion would be a bigger driver of inflows than the tax measures alone.

In the weeks before the announcement, India's finance minister personally met with RBI officials to push for Bloomberg index entry, a government official confirmed.

## What NRIs Should Know

For NRI investors, the reforms open several practical doors.

First, the expansion of the Fully Accessible Route means a wider range of Indian government securities are now available without caps — potentially allowing NRIs to build more diversified fixed-income positions in Indian debt.

Second, the FCNR deposit incentive, which was already offering rates near 7 per cent on dollar deposits at Indian banks, is now paired with broader capital account liberalisation. Together, these measures aim to attract the estimated $300 billion in NRI deposits that Indian banks have historically competed for.

Third, Citi has sharply revised India's balance of payments forecast for the current fiscal year to a $5 billion surplus, compared with an earlier projected deficit of $60 billion. If that projection holds, it would underpin the rupee and make the carry trade in Indian bonds — already attractive at 7 per cent-plus yields — more compelling.

## The Risks That Remain

Not everyone is convinced. Rong Ren Goh, head of macro and thematics for Asian fixed income at Eastspring Investments, warned that the rupee's trajectory remains the bigger issue for offshore investors. "Investors are likely to wait for clearer signs of rupee stability before raising allocations," he said.

The broader investment backdrop for bonds remains challenging, with high global interest-rate volatility and inflationary pressures from energy and food prices. M&G Investments' Low Guan Yi noted that "the shift from monetary easing to tightening" across many markets adds uncertainty for fixed income globally.

UBS Asset Management, which remains neutral to underweight on Indian fixed income, acknowledged the positive signal but said it would monitor the situation before making material allocation changes.

For NRI investors weighing India's government bond market, the opportunity is clearer than it has been in years. Whether the currency risk cooperates will determine whether this moment becomes a turning point or another near-miss.

*Sources: Reuters; Reserve Bank of India; Bloomberg; Citi Research; Livemint*
